en.title: Netflix's 'The Final Problem' Channels Classic Holmes on a Spanish Island
en.summary: A celebrated Spanish actor steps into the shoes of a fictional detective, only to find himself embroiled in a very real murder mystery. This four-episode miniseries promises a classic whodunit with a meta twist.
en.body:
Get ready for a classic murder mystery served with a side of meta-commentary. Netflix's latest Spanish import, **The Final Problem**, plunges viewers into a secluded island setting where a series of suspicious deaths mirrors the very stories its protagonist once brought to life. Premiering on September 25, 2026, this four-episode miniseries adapts Arturo Pérez-Reverte's novel, offering a compact yet compelling whodunit for binge-watchers.

The story centers on **Benjamin Basil** (played by the venerable **José Coronado**), an aging Spanish actor whose career highlight was portraying Sherlock Holmes in a series of film adaptations. Now somewhat adrift and barely sober, Basil finds himself on the remote Santa Agueda island off the coast of Mallorca. He's there to discuss a potential new role with a producer friend, but the idyllic setting quickly sours when a stormy night reveals a body hanging from a rope. What initially appears to be a suicide is, through Basil's keen, Holmes-esque observations, quickly revealed to be murder. With a cast of bourgeois suspects, including a new starlet and the no-nonsense hotel manager, no one is safe, and Basil must channel his iconic detective persona to uncover the truth.

## A Method Actor's Mystery

The core conceit of **The Final Problem** is brilliant: an actor who has *played* Sherlock Holmes now finds himself in a situation demanding the detective's legendary deductive skills. This isn't just a man investigating a crime; it's a performer embodying his most famous role to survive. **José Coronado**, known for his commanding presence in shows like **The Snow Girl**, brings a seasoned gravitas to Basil, making the transition from actor to amateur sleuth utterly believable. The ensemble cast, including **Maribel Verdú** as the formidable Mrs. Ausländer and **Martiño Rivas** as the aspiring crime novelist Francisco Foxá, adds further depth to the confined setting, where every character harbors potential secrets.

## Island of Secrets and Suspicion

**The Final Problem** leans into the tropes of classic Agatha Christie-style mysteries, but with a distinctly Spanish flair and the added layer of its lead's unique background. The isolated island setting is crucial, trapping the characters together and amplifying the tension with each passing hour. As Basil delves deeper, the line between his celebrated past and the perilous present blurs. The series promises a tightly plotted narrative, where the claustrophobic environment and the limited suspect pool create an intense atmosphere. Fans of intricate puzzles and character-driven thrillers will find much to savor as they try to piece together the clues alongside Basil.

## What's Next

With its compact four-episode run, **The Final Problem** is perfectly suited for a weekend binge. Viewers can expect a satisfying conclusion that ties up the mystery while exploring the fascinating psychological landscape of its protagonist. Keep an eye out for further details on potential international availability beyond Netflix's initial release on September 25, 2026.

content_raw: Picture Credit: Netflix A small remote island, a series of murders, a detective, and a number of bourgeois suspects (yes, and the maid): sounds familiar? If it is, then you already know what to look for in this new prestige, 4-episode miniseries out of Spain : a good (very) old-fashioned murder mystery. But does all evidence point towards a good watch? José Coronado ( Innocent, The Snow Girl ) brings his decades-old honed chops into the main character of Benjamin Basil, an aging Spanish actor, who once claimed fame as Sherlock Holmes in a series of Conan Doyle film adaptations. On the outs from Hollywood and barely sober, he follows a producer friend, Fonseca ( Gonzalo De Castro ), to discuss a potential new role on his boat… and ends up on Santa Agueda island, off the coast of Mallorca, in a remote establishment managed by no-nonsense, mannered Mrs. Ausländer ( Maribel Verdú ). There, he must indulge the abrasive character of Fonseca and his new starlet girlfriend Vicky ( Cristina Kovani ), and meets aspiring crime novelist Francisco Foxá ( Martiño Rivas ). But then, after a stormy night, a body hanging from a rope is discovered. What is thought to be a suicide, through a few observations from Benjamin, soon turns out to be a murder, with no one safe in the hotel. Let the games begin… To somewhat enjoy the short 4-episode run of The Final Problem , one must buy into the idea of a veteran actor having played Sherlock Holmes a dozen times going full method. That is, as preparation, getting to master the keen, almost supernatural senses of observation of the legendary detective, and apply it to have some strong deductions and knowledge on any person he meets. This is the main twist of the project: “He is not Holmes, he just played it several times in movies!” But it seems like writers of this adaptation of a bestselling book ( Alberto Macías , Carlos Molinero and Marisol Farré ) do not intend to play into the meta aspect: Basil is Holmesian in his demeanor and findings, and soon the hotel depends on his undeniable skills to shed light on the happenings on the island as the arrival of the police is (of course) delayed. Nothing really happens with the conceit: Basil does not use his status to stroke his actor’s ego, or get mocked or dismissed by other characters. Instead, The Final Problem plays its mystery partition frustratingly straight. On the platform which brought us the sequels to Knives Out , that is certainly a choice. Picture Credit: Netflix Part of the fun of these mysteries, in movies or a series, is to assemble a tapestry of characters playing suspect and sometimes (not always) hamming it up. Alas, even with all his screentime, the Watson to Basil’s Sherlock barely registers: as Foxá eventually raises concerns or suspicions towards our amateur sleuth, the character is not either duplicitous or sympathetic enough to hold weight.
